findings.explanation: The module creates a regional policy and a default-deny ingress rule on it, but there is no google_compute_region_network_firewall_policy_association. The global policy gets one (google_compute_network_firewall_policy_association.main). An unassociated policy is inert, so the regional deny_ingress rule at priority 65000 never evaluates traffic. Consumers reading the README ('a regional network firewall policy') reasonably assume it is enforced.
findings.remediation: Add a google_compute_region_network_firewall_policy_association attaching the regional policy to var.network in var.region, or document explicitly that the caller is responsible for associating it.
findings.title: Regional network firewall policy is created but never associated with a network

findings.explanation: The README tells consumers to add their own rules above priority 65000, but every rule resource inside this module sets firewall_policy = <policy>.name, not .id (see google_compute_network_firewall_policy_rule.allow_health_checks:2). The module exports only .id, so a consumer cannot wire up an extra google_compute_network_firewall_policy_rule without re-deriving the name by string concatenation.
findings.remediation: Add name outputs alongside the id outputs for all three policies.
findings.title: Outputs expose only policy IDs, but rule resources need the policy name

findings.explanation: deny_egress (0.0.0.0/0, ip_protocol all) and deny_ingress (0.0.0.0/0, ip_protocol all) both set enable_logging = true as a literal. Catch-all deny rules on a busy VPC are the highest-volume rules in the policy, and every hit becomes a Cloud Logging entry billed at ingestion. There is no variable to turn this off or scope it, so a consumer who only wants the allow rules logged has to fork the module.
findings.remediation: Introduce a variable (e.g. var.log_denied_traffic, default true) driving enable_logging on the two catch-all deny rules, so the security-useful default is kept but the cost is controllable. Note HLD_GCP_367 requires logging on firewall policy rules, so any default other than true needs a holden:ignore justification.
findings.title: Logging is hardcoded on for catch-all deny rules with no way to disable it

findings.explanation: Priorities 1000 (allow_health_checks, deny_rdp) and 65000 (deny_egress, deny_ingress) are literals. Priorities are unique per policy in GCP, so a consumer adding their own rule at 1000 gets an apply-time API error and has no module knob to move the built-in rule out of the way.
findings.remediation: Expose the priorities as variables with the current values as defaults, e.g. var.health_check_priority = 1000 and var.default_deny_priority = 65000.
findings.title: Rule priorities are hardcoded, so consumers cannot avoid collisions

findings.explanation: count = var.parent == "" ? 0 : 1 appears in both google_compute_firewall_policy.hierarchical.tf:2 and google_compute_firewall_policy_rule.deny_rdp.tf:2. The rule indexes hierarchical[0] unconditionally, so if the two expressions ever drift the rule fails at plan time with an index error rather than a clear message.
findings.remediation: Extract to a local (local.create_hierarchical = var.parent != "") and use count = local.create_hierarchical ? 1 : 0 in both places.
findings.title: Hierarchical count guard is duplicated across two files

findings.explanation: example/examplea is the only example and omits var.parent, so google_compute_firewall_policy.hierarchical and google_compute_firewall_policy_rule.deny_rdp are always count = 0 in CI. Two of the module's seven resources, plus the try() in hierarchical_policy_id, are never validated or planned.
findings.remediation: Add a second example (example/exampleb) that sets parent, or make parent settable via a tfvars in CI. A hierarchical policy needs roles/compute.orgSecurityResourceAdmin, so a plan-only check may be the practical ceiling.
findings.title: The hierarchical code path is never exercised by an example

suggested_policies.rationale: GCP firewall policy rules have no name attribute, only a numeric priority, so the description field is the only place the intent of a rule is recorded. A rule without one is unreviewable in the console and in a plan diff. This is a concrete, unambiguous attribute check across the three rule resource types, and holden currently has only HLD_GCP_367 (logging) on these types.
suggested_policies.yaml:
id: HLD_GCP_XXX
name: Firewall policy rules should have a description
principle: maintainability
severity: LOW
rationale: |
  GCP firewall policy rules are identified only by a numeric priority; they have
  no name. Without a description there is nothing in the console, the API, or a
  Terraform plan diff that records why the rule exists, which makes review and
  safe removal of stale rules impossible.
remediation: |
  Add a description to each rule:
    resource "google_compute_network_firewall_policy_rule" "example" {
      priority    = 1000
      description = "Google load balancer health check probes"
      ...
    }
resources:
  google_compute_network_firewall_policy_rule:
    path: description
    not_null: true
  google_compute_region_network_firewall_policy_rule:
    path: description
    not_null: true
  google_compute_firewall_policy_rule:
    path: description
    not_null: true
